checkpoints.note: First farming-based population growth; Egypt's Nile floodplain already supports the map's densest cluster.
Old Kingdom Egypt's pyramid-building state is the map's first true demographic and fiscal concentration; Europe still thinly settled.
Middle Kingdom Egypt recovers from the First Intermediate Period; Minoan Crete's first palaces mark the Aegean's takeoff.
Palatial Bronze Age growth: Egypt, the Hittites and the Minoans all expand on irrigated or palace-redistributed surplus.
Late Bronze Age population peak just before the palatial world's systemic collapse.
Post-collapse recovery still incomplete in the east (Aegean/Anatolia lost most of their Bronze Age peak c.1100-1000 BCE); Iron Age farming pushes numbers up in temperate Europe regardless.
Classical urbanization: Persian satrapal wealth, Greek poleis and an expanding Carthage all growing on trade and grain surplus.
Hellenistic and Punic Mediterranean at its commercial height, just before Rome's conquests absorb it wholesale.
Augustan peace unifies almost the entire map under one administration; monetized, tax-fed growth follows.
Roman demographic plateau near its ancient peak, but the Antonine Plague (165-180) has already cut the growth rate.
Crisis-of-the-3rd-century plagues, civil wars and Germanic migrations reverse two centuries of Roman growth.
Justinianic Plague (from 541) and endless Byzantine-Sassanid war produce antiquity's deepest population trough.
Carolingian agricultural revival in the west; Abbasid-era prosperity lifts Egypt and the Levant.
The medieval climate optimum begins a long, nearly unbroken expansion across the whole map.
High medieval takeoff: three-field rotation, forest clearance and the commercial revolution drive Europe past 55 million.
Medieval population ceiling reached just before catastrophe; Europe, Egypt and the Levant are all near their pre-modern peaks.
The Black Death (1347-51) and its recurring waves cut roughly a third off the map's population within two generations.
Renaissance-era recovery is essentially complete north of the Alps; Ottoman conquests reorganize the eastern rim.
Ottoman and Habsburg territorial peaks coincide with steady population growth, though not yet back above the pre-Black-Death growth rate.
Growth slows overall: the Ottoman core stagnates and France plateaus, while Russia and England begin accelerating.
Pre-industrial demographic take-off begins in Britain and Russia; most of the map is still Malthusian.
The agricultural and early industrial revolution breaks the old Malthusian ceiling in northwest Europe first.
Industrializing Europe adds nearly 80 million in a single generation; Egypt's Muhammad Ali-era cotton boom also drives fast growth.
Second Industrial Revolution and public-health gains drive the fastest sustained growth the map has ever recorded.
Peak of the first globalization era; mass emigration to the Americas is the only real brake on European growth.
WWI (~17M dead) and the 1918-20 flu slow growth sharply; the USSR's collectivization famines are just ahead.
Postwar count: WWII killed roughly 40 million Europeans including the Holocaust, a loss the following baby boom already masks here.
Postwar baby boom plus the Green Revolution in Egypt/Maghreb/Anatolia drive the fastest map-wide growth on record.
European growth has nearly stopped (below-replacement fertility almost everywhere) while Egypt, the Maghreb and Anatolia keep booming.
Europe's population has plateaued or begun to shrink; almost all further map growth now comes from Egypt, the Maghreb and Anatolia.

wealthEras.note: Egypt's Nile floodplain surplus creates the map's first great concentration of wealth; nothing else on the map comes close.
Palace-temple redistribution economies (Egypt, Hittites, Minoans, Mycenaeans) hoard bronze-trade wealth; commoners see little of it.
Phoenician city-states (Tyre, Sidon, then Carthage) monopolize Mediterranean maritime trade in metal, purple dye and timber.
Wealth spreads to Greek poleis (Athens' silver/trade empire) and to Achaemenid satrapal taxation of Anatolia and the Levant.
Ptolemaic Egypt's royal monopolies on grain, papyrus and Red Sea trade, plus Rhodian/Pergamene commerce, mark the era's wealth peaks.
Pax Romana taxes and trades almost the whole map as one unit; Italian elites, Alexandria and Antioch concentrate the surplus.
Constantinople's gold solidus and the Baghdad-centered Abbasid economy, radiating into Egypt and the Levant, dwarf a poor, rural Latin West.
Fatimid/Ayyubid Cairo's Red Sea spice trade, Venetian and Genoese maritime commerce, and trans-Saharan Almoravid gold define the era's wealth.
Mamluk Egypt taxes the world's spice trade at its Red Sea chokepoint; Venice and Florentine banking are its main European partners.
Spanish American silver inflates prices without building lasting wealth; the Dutch Republic becomes the era's genuinely richest society per capita.
Britain's agricultural then industrial revolution overtakes the Dutch per-capita lead by the 1840s and pulls decisively ahead.
Germany, Britain, France and Belgium build steel, chemical and electrical industries; Britain still leads world finance and shipping.
Two world wars, hyperinflation and the Depression destroy capital repeatedly; the United States (off-map) becomes the world's wealthiest economy.
Marshall Plan reconstruction fuels West German, French and Benelux 'economic miracles'; the Communist bloc stagnates behind separate pricing.
Northwest/Nordic Europe (Switzerland, Norway, Ireland, Germany) leads per-capita wealth; Egypt, the Maghreb and the Levant remain far poorer despite much faster population growth.

uncertainties: 1 CE / 200 CE Roman Empire population is the single biggest ancient dispute: modern estimates range roughly 45-76 million depending on assumed Egyptian and Anatolian densities; I used a mid estimate (~55-58M) rather than Beloch's low end or Russell/Frier's higher end.

Bronze Age Collapse (c.1200-1000 BCE) demographic impact is not directly visible between the -1200 and -800 checkpoints (no intervening year); the Aegean/Anatolia likely lost 50-90% of local Late Bronze Age population by c.1000 BCE before recovering, masked here by continued growth in unaffected temperate Europe.

Justinianic Plague (541 CE onward) severity is actively disputed: the traditional view (Russell, McCormick) holds it killed a third to half of the Mediterranean population; revisionists (Mordechai & Eisenberg, 2019) argue textual sources are overstated and archaeological/palynological evidence shows no comparable collapse. I followed the traditional (higher-mortality) view for the 600 CE trough but flag it as contested.

Black Death mortality (1347-51) is usually cited as 30-50% of Europe's population, with some post-2004 scholarship (Benedictow) arguing for ~50% and worst-hit regions (England, Norway) losing 60-70%. I used an aggregate ~30% Europe-wide drop between 1340 and 1400, which is conservative relative to the highest estimates.

Ptolemaic/Roman Egypt population is disputed between low modern estimates (~4-5 million, Scheidel/Bagnall-Frier) and high ancient literary figures (Diodorus ~7M free residents, Josephus ~7.5M excluding Alexandria); I followed the modern low estimate.

Achaemenid Persia's total imperial population (used for the -400 majorPolities entry) is wildly uncertain in the literature, with published figures ranging from ~17 million to over 50 million; 25M is a rough compromise, not a consensus figure.

Pre-1881 Ottoman Empire population figures (used at 1500-1800) rest on tax-register extrapolation, not census, since the first real Ottoman census was 1881-93; my 1600/1700 figures reconcile a '30M in 1600' aggregate estimate against a lower '~21M Asian+European' 1700 estimate, implying real 17th-century stagnation/decline that is itself debated.

Egypt's population c.1800 is cited as low as ~2.5M (first modern/French-survey era count) and as high as ~4.5M in some secondary literature; I used 3.0M, closer to the lower end, which affects how dramatic the 1800-1900 cotton-boom growth looks.

europePopulation for 1900-2025 follows the common demographic convention of counting Russia's population wholly within 'Europe' (the standard UN Population Division regional grouping) rather than splitting out Asian Russia/Siberia; a stricter 'European Russia only' definition would run several tens of millions lower at each modern checkpoint.

McEvedy & Jones (1978) is the backbone source for most pre-1800 figures on this file, but is itself, by modern historiographical consensus, an extrapolation from very thin evidence for most pre-Roman and post-Roman dates; treat all checkpoints before 1500 as order-of-magnitude estimates, not precise counts.

1913 and 1930 Europe totals are reconstructed from a c.1900 anchor (408M) and c.1950 anchor (549M) using plausible pre-/post-WWI growth rates rather than a single authoritative published table; exact contemporaneous figures vary by several percent across sources (Maddison's 'Greater Europe' figures also include overseas European-settler populations and are not directly comparable).

1975/2000 Anatolia, Levant and Maghreb sub-totals are built up from national population series (Turkey, Syria, Lebanon, Israel, Jordan, Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya) rather than a single regional source, so rounding/consistency errors of a few percent are likely in the mapPopulation totals for those years.
